mr.clean takes the three CSV files, loops through them, sets negative pollutant             measurements equal to 0, converts dates from slashed to hyphenated if they are 
not already hyphenated, and expects an input after the input CSV to determine
whether to calculate ozone concentrations in parts per million or parts per
billion. It then deletes duplicate rows for consistency to ensure that there is
only one row per date.

# Cleaned Frame
```{r mr clean}
AQ_2018 <- read.csv("AQ_2018.csv")
AQ_2019 <- read.csv("AQ_2019.csv")
AQ_2020 <- read.csv("AQ_2020.csv")
filename <- AQ_2018



mr.clean <- function(filename = "AQ_2018.csv", units = "ppm"){
  
  # Import the file
  data <- read.csv(filename)
 
  #Renaming columns inside the function for convenience
  data <- rename(data, co_conc = 'Daily.Max.8.hour.CO.Concentration')
  data <- rename(data, pm_conc = 'Daily.Mean.PM2.5.Concentration')
  data <- rename(data, o3_conc = 'Daily.Max.8.hour.Ozone.Concentration')
  
  # Loop through each value and set negative values
  for(i in 1:nrow(data)){
    # Neutralize negatives for carbon monoxide
    if(data$co_conc[i] < 0 & !is.na(data$co_conc[i])){
      data$co_conc[i] <- 0
    }
    # Neutralize negatives for particulate matter
    if(data$pm_conc[i] < 0 & !is.na(data$pm_conc[i])){
      data$pm_conc[i] <- 0
    }
    # Neutralize negatives for ozone
    if(data$o3_conc[i] < 0 & !is.na(data$o3_conc[i])){
      data$pm_conc[i] <- 0
    }
  }

  
  # Convert date
  data <- data |>
    mutate(Date = mdy(Date))
 
   #Let the user change between parts per million and parts per billion
  if(units == "ppb"){
    data$o3_conc = data$o3_conc * 1000
  }  
  
  #Average duplicate measures, delete duplicate rows
  filename_sum <- data |>
    group_by(Date) |>
    summarize(
      average_co = mean(co_conc, na.rm = TRUE),
      average_pm = mean(pm_conc, na.rm = TRUE),
      average_o3 = mean(o3_conc, na.rm = TRUE) 
      )
    
  

  
  # Return the final data frame
  return(filename_sum)
  
  
}

```

```{r run }
#Run function
mr.clean("AQ_2018.csv", "ppm")
mr.clean("AQ_2018.csv", "ppb")
View(mr.clean("AQ_2018.csv", "ppm"))

View(mr.clean("AQ_2019.csv"))
View(mr.clean("AQ_2020.csv", "ppm"))

mr.clean("AQ_2020.csv", "ppm")

```

#Producing a Unified Dataset
```{r unified dataset}
clean_18 <- mr.clean("AQ_2018.csv")
clean_19 <- mr.clean("AQ_2019.csv")
clean_20 <- mr.clean("AQ_2020.csv")
#I need to combine all of the sets to make a big set for all of the
#pollutants across all three years.
full_set <- rbind(clean_18, clean_19, clean_20)
```

#Making the tables legible by changing variable names and cutting decimals
#down to three points.

I have run into another issue where I can only get parts per million in my
table even if I ask Mr. Clean for parts per billion.
```{r tables}
library(gtsummary)


#Tables of pollutant averages, minima, and maxima for each year.
clean_18 |>
  select(average_co, average_pm, average_o3) |>
  tbl_summary(
    missing = "no",
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({min}, {max})",
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 3,
    label = list(
      average_co ~ "Carbon Monoxide",
      average_pm ~ "PM2.5",
      average_o3 ~ "Ozone"
    )
  ) |>
  modify_header(label = "**Pollutant**") |>
  modify_caption("Raleigh-Durham Airport: Average Pollutant Levels Table January
                 1 Through December 31 2018")

clean_19 |>
  select(average_co, average_pm, average_o3) |>
  tbl_summary(
    missing = "no",
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({min}, {max})",
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 3,
    label = list(
      average_co ~ "Carbon Monoxide",
      average_pm ~ "PM2.5",
      average_o3 ~ "Ozone"
    )
  ) |>
  modify_header(label = "**Pollutant**") |>
  modify_caption("Raleigh-Durham Airport: Average Pollutant Levels Table January
                 1 Through December 31 2019")

clean_20 |>
  select(average_co, average_pm, average_o3) |>
  tbl_summary(
    missing = "no",
    type = everything() ~ "continuous",
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({min}, {max})",
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 3,
    label = list(
      average_co ~ "Carbon Monoxide",
      average_pm ~ "PM2.5",
      average_o3 ~ "Ozone"
    )
  ) |>
  modify_header(label = "**Pollutant**") |>
  modify_caption("Raleigh-Durham Airport: Average Pollutant Levels Table 
                 January 1 Through April 30 2020")


```

           
#Plot 1: CO and Ozone by Month
```{r plot1}
  
#Put this code in an e-mail (i.e. the ENTIRE chunk)


#Crash and burn 1: Just start by making a box plot. Add error bars later.

library(lubridate)
full_set$month = month(full_set$Date)
full_set$year = year(full_set$Date)

#Only run if you want ozone in parts per hundred million.
#full_set$average_o3 <-
  #full_set$average_o3 * 100

#Create confidence interval data
 full_plot1 <- full_set |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(average_co, average_o3),
    names_to = "pollutant",
    values_to = "concentration"
  ) |>
  group_by(month, pollutant) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    lower = mean - 1.96 * se,
    upper = mean + 1.96 * se,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) 

#I also need to change the display for the factor to something more presentable,
#but I cannot figure out how.
ggplot(full_plot1, aes(x = factor(month), 
                       y = mean, ymin = lower, ymax = upper,
                       color = factor(pollutant))) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.5) +
  xlab("Month") +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
               "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "CO Concentration (ppm)",
    limits = c(0, 0.6), 
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ . * 1000,
      name = "O3 Concentration (ppm)"
    )
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.6)) +
  ggtitle("Average Concentration of Carbon Monoxide and Ozone by Month from 2018 to 2020") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "average_co" = "purple",
      "average_o3" = "limegreen"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "average_co" = "CO",
      "average_o3" = "O3"
    )
  )


 


#Maybe ask AI how to make separate plots for these two pollutants with
#separate autoscales
```
Unit of Choice: ppm for both. CO concentrations are about ten times as high as
ozone concentrations. If I were to multiple ozone by a thousand to get parts per
billion when I do not have a part in my program to ajust CO to parts per ten
million or hundred million, it should be easiest to read the graph if I keep
everything in parts per million.

Why a Scatter Plot?: The rules for the plot called for an average for each
month, but I could not get boxplots by month separate for each pollutant, but
I could get separate month-by-pollutant average dots on a scatter plot to
communicate the average concentration by pollutant for each month.

Why Purple and Lime Green: The reason for this was to pick colors that are far
apart and that someone with a colorblindness condition should not confuse.

Interpretation of Plot 1: Carbon monoxide levels are lowest in the months from
May to July. They increase in the fall up to a peak in December before gradually
decreasing until they reach that May-to-July bottom. Because the ozone concentrations are so much lower than CO concentrations, it is difficult to tell. (DNF)

#Plot 2: PM2.5 by Month and Year (Should I just ditch the in ppm label just
in case some weirdo wants to pick parts per billion?)
```{r plot2}
#For the initial crash and burn, at least try to get month on the x-axis
#and PM2.5 concentration on the y axis.

full_plot2 <- full_set |>
  group_by(month, year) |>
  summarize(monthmean_pm = mean(average_pm, na.rm = TRUE)
            
            #come back and figure out how to
            #code those error bars
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(monthmean_pm),
    names_to = "pollutant",
    values_to = "concentration"
  )
  
#Scatter plot was the only thing that I could get to work.



ggplot(full_plot2, aes(x = factor(month), y = concentration, 
                       #ymin = lower, ymax = upper,
                       color = factor(year))) + 
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(aes(group = year)) +
  xlab("Month") +
  ylab("Pollutant Concentration (ug/m^3)") +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
               "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 12)) +
  ggtitle("Average Concentration of PM2.5 in Micrograms Per Cubic Meter
          By Month from 2018 to 2020") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "gold"))
```

Why a scatterplot?: For this figure, I was told to display every month-and-year
subgroup. That is 28 subgroups. When there are a lot of dots that need to be
plotted, that is a job for a boxplot.

Why red, blue, and gold?: I am unaware of any sort of colorblindness or other
visual impairment that should make it difficult to distinguish between the dots.
They should be so distinct that anyone could distinguish between them.


Interpretation of Plot 2: There is no link between time of the year and 
PM2.5 concentration.

with 10 or fewer entries as categorical. I forgot how to truncate decimal

add to truncate all decimals to three places past the point. 

I forgot the function for setting colors, so I asked Gemini what they were with
